strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a practical clinical NLP resource gap with 8,767 shareable synthetic snippets, covering 13 SBDH categories plus pain and transitions of care, and providing spans, presence, temporality, and rationales.

The experiments provide credible evidence that synthetic pretraining benefits small-model classification. Evaluations span two clinical datasets, several architectures, and three independent runs, with substantial improvements on MIMIC-SBDH. These supported results and the resource contribution warrant Findings.

The substantial expert audit of 1,755 examples, adjudication, corrected test annotations, and category-level error analysis are valuable. Generation prompts, seed examples, annotation guidelines, training configurations, and links to released materials support reuse and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benefits are less general than the abstract and conclusion suggest. Encoder NER gains are negligible, VA Mamba classification gains are absent or minimal, and the Llama experiments show little benefit. The headline 94.44-point improvement concerns housing insecurity with only 18 positive test examples; variation across training seeds does not capture uncertainty from this small test sample.

The comparison against alternative pretraining is unclear. Appendix D.2 claims a budget-matched comparison with MIMIC-SBDH pretraining, but Table 13 supplies only one unspecified baseline per model and is also used for the no-synthetic comparison in D.1. Separate results are needed. Oversampling or class-weighted baselines would also clarify how much rare-category improvement exceeds simpler imbalance remedies. The largest NER gain relies on a highly unstable T5 baseline.

The annotation audit has limitations as evidence of independent reference quality. Experts review existing GPT-4 labels, and Appendix E.2 accepts any plausible GPT-selected category for ambiguous spans while assigning a more specific category to newly added annotations. This makes reference labels dependent on the initial output. The 71.06% agreement also includes added annotations in its denominator, whereas the 90.78% LLM audit excludes omission detection; these figures should be distinguished explicitly.

Several distinctive dataset attributes receive limited downstream validation. Experiments retain only presence=yes annotations and do not evaluate temporal prediction. Rationale supervision improves macro-F by only 0.66 and 0.58 points for the base models, with the latter nonsignificant, and evaluation remains on synthetic text. This supports a modest auxiliary-training benefit but does not establish the claimed transfer of reasoning capability to real clinical extraction.

Reproducibility documentation needs clarification around downstream classification prompts and verbalizers, the statistical tests underlying reported p-values, and the deduplication rule stated as similarity to 'all' previous examples. Access restrictions on VA-SBDH additionally limit independent reproduction of the real-data NER results.

The corpus's average length of 13.7 words and acknowledged lack of common clinical formatting constrain its representativeness. Some expert-endorsed inferences also deserve scrutiny: Appendix E.4 treats working two jobs as evidence of financial insecurity without explicit financial difficulty. Auditing such assumptions would strengthen the resource's construct validity and the case for broader clinical applicability.
